card.h1: Ozone Policy as a Supply Regime: What the HFC Phasedown Does to Cooling-Exposed Assets
The ozone regime is now a government-administered scarcity machine, and the pricing effects are already in reported results

ul.li: Situation. Montreal Protocol machinery has been retargeted from ozone to climate. The AIM Act phases down US HFC production and consumption 85% by 2036; the Senate ratified the Kigali Amendment in September 2022

Complication. A phasedown caps supply of a chemical class without capping demand for the cooling it provides. Chemours' Thermal & Specialized Solutions posted Q1 2026 net sales of $568M, up 22%, with segment EBITDA up 35% and margins at 33%

Resolution. Our read: the transmission channels are producer pricing power in a concentrated fluorochemical market, input-cost pass-through in cooling-intensive businesses, and a reclaim market the EU rules explicitly advantage

What this briefing is not. No portfolio holdings, weights or valuations were supplied for this paper. Every portfolio statement here is a labeled hypothesis or a diligence question, not a position read

card.p: Reading convention: sourced claims are stated flat; derived arithmetic is marked illustrative; our inferences are marked as ours.

card.h1: Part I — Why this treaty is the one regime that reliably binds
The Montreal Protocol is the rare treaty that delivered, which is why its schedules behave like a maturity ladder

ul.li: Nearly 99% of banned ozone-depleting substances have been phased out globally

The 2025 Antarctic ozone hole ranked fourth-to-fifth smallest since severe depletion began in 1992; maximum ozone mass deficit was 36.7 million tons on 29 September, more than 25% below the 1990–2010 mean of 50.1 million tons
Recovery to 1980 values is projected around 2066 over the Antarctic, 2045 over the Arctic, and 2040 for the rest of the world
The phaseout also avoided roughly 0.5°C of warming, which is how the treaty acquired its second mandate

card.p: Our read: schedules that have held for four decades across changes of government carry less political risk than most regulatory exposure, and can be underwritten on their dates.

card.h1: Each substitution cycle moved value to the owner of the replacement molecule, and the phase-out dates differ sharply by jurisdiction

ul.li: The 1987 Protocol drove a large increase in HFC use; HFCs were then regarded as acceptable CFC substitutes
HFCs have no known natural sources and global warming potentials hundreds to thousands of times that of CO₂
The 2016 Kigali Amendment brought HFCs inside the same quota-and-schedule apparatus

HCFCs, corrected. Developed (non-Article 5) parties reached 100% consumption reduction on 1 January 2020, with a 0.5% servicing allowance running to 2030. Developing (Article 5) parties reach 100% on 1 January 2030, with a further 2.5% servicing tail averaged over 2030–2040, so HCFC servicing demand persists to 1 January 2040

card.p: Why the correction matters: "HCFCs gone by 2030" overstates the cliff. The installed-base servicing tail is a ten-year revenue window in Article 5 markets, and it is where the equipment replacement cycle actually lands.

card.h1: Part II — The machinery, and the 2026 divergence between the two largest markets
Three levers do the work: a production cap, sector-by-sector transition rules, and a reclaim mandate

ol.li: Allowance allocation. EPA must determine production and consumption allowances by 1 October each year for the following year; allowances are tradeable and transferable, and EPA has withheld, retired or revoked allowances from named entities as administrative consequences
Technology Transitions. Subsection (i) authorises EPA to restrict a regulated substance fully, partially, or on a graduated schedule within a named sector or subsector
Emissions reduction and reclamation. Leak repair, reclamation and technician rules that turn waste gas into a regulated feedstock

card.p: Our read: this is an industrial policy stack, not a ban. The cap creates scarcity, sector rules set the timing of demand destruction, and reclaim rules decide who may monetise the installed base.

card.h1: In 2026 the two largest markets moved in opposite directions, and only the sector timing moved

ul.li: United States, loosening. EPA's final rule of 26 May 2026, effective 27 July 2026, relaxes Technology Transitions requirements across intermodal refrigerated transport, semiconductor process refrigeration and chillers, supermarket and remote condensing systems, cold storage warehouses, and refrigerated laboratory equipment, and permits continued installation of pre-2025 residential and light commercial AC and heat pump inventory
The action formed part of deregulatory measures announced 12 March 2025 in response to industry petitions for reconsideration

European Union, tightening. Regulation (EU) 2024/573 replaced the 2014 F-gas regime. Its quota system governs the placing on the market of hydrofluorocarbons, and from the 2026 allocation year quota carries a payment
The cap is untouched. The 85% US phasedown to 2036 is statutory

card.h1: The EU charge is a payment for HFC quota, not a levy on every F-gas, and the scope boundary is the whole point
card.p: What the rule actually says. Article 16(1) allows HFCs to be placed on the market only against quota allocated by the Commission, and Article 17(5) makes that allocation subject to payment of EUR 3 for each tonne of CO₂ equivalent of quota allocated. The Commission's FAQ confirms producers and importers pay from 2025 in respect of quota for 2026 onward

ul.li: In scope: hydrofluorocarbons listed in Annex I, Section 1, alone or in mixtures
Out of scope: other F-gases including PFCs, SF₆ and NF₃, and quota allocated before 2026
R1234yf sits in Annex II as an unsaturated compound with GWP 0.501, outside the Annex I HFC quota system, so it bears no quota allocation payment at all
No indexation is stated. EUR 3 per tonne CO₂e is a fixed statutory figure; the FAQ and Regulation say nothing about escalation, so a permanent indexed levy should not be assumed

card.p: Illustrative arithmetic, Annex I bulk HFCs only. At EUR 3 per tonne CO₂e, quota cost per kilogram is 0.003 × GWP: about €4.29/kg for R134a at GWP 1,430 and about €2.09/kg for a GWP-697 blend. This is our calculation from the statutory rate, incurred at allocation rather than per sale, and for blends it depends on the Annex I content. It is not a published price list.
Interpretation, ours. The commercial edge for Annex II gases is a scope exclusion, not a measurable per-kilogram tariff differential, and the earlier "2,000-fold advantage" framing is withdrawn.

card.h1: Part III — Where the money is visibly moving
Two producers are converting the phasedown into margin, and it is visible in four quarters of reported results

ul.li: Chemours TSS, Q1 2026: net sales $568M, up 22% year over year; Opteon refrigerants $313M, up 12%; Freon $162M, up 67% on North American automotive demand; segment EBITDA up 35%, margins 33%
Full-year 2025: a record TSS performance driven by a 56% increase in Opteon sales, against flat group net sales of $5.8bn
Solstice, Q1 2026: $711M, up 19% on price and volume, attributed to the HFO transition and data-centre demand
Solstice 2025: refrigerant net sales up 16% on low-GWP adoption; group net sales $3.9bn, up 3%

card.p: Our read: group revenue is flat while the regulated segment compounds. The phasedown is concentrating these businesses rather than lifting them.

card.h1: Legacy gas prices are holding, and the quota market clears well above the statutory allocation rate

ul.li: European prices for high-GWP gases rose slightly in Q2 2026: R134a and R410A each up 1% year over year, and up 1% and 2% respectively on Q1
Among alternatives, R290 rose 11%, R32 9%, and R448A 4% on the quarter
Quota permit prices ranged €14 to €18.50 per tonne CO₂e, averaging €17.19, down 2% on Q1
Reclaimed R404A fell 9% on the quarter among service companies and 4% among distributors

card.p: Two interpretations, ours. First, the secondary quota market clears at roughly five times the EUR 3 statutory allocation payment, so scarcity value, not the administrative fee, is what sets the economics. Second, the installed base keeps paying to run, which makes servicing revenue stickier than phaseout headlines imply.

card.h1: Compute growth is a thermal-load problem, and it competes for the same constrained molecules

ul.li: Solstice attributes refrigerant strength partly to growing data-centre demand, alongside nuclear and electronic materials, citing AI, data centres, semiconductor manufacturing and nuclear energy as secular drivers
EPA's 2026 reconsideration specifically addressed industrial process refrigeration and chillers used in semiconductor manufacturing
A statutory supply cap legislated in 2020 now meets a build cycle that post-dates the assumptions behind it

card.p: Diligence question, not a finding. Do any of our infrastructure and chemicals exposures share a refrigerant-availability dependency that neither book currently tracks? We cannot answer this without holdings data. Proposed test: identify positions whose cost base or delivery schedule depends on regulated refrigerant supply, and measure the overlap.

card.h1: Four things would break this thesis, and three are already observable

ul.li: Substitution past the incumbents. Natural refrigerants such as R290 propane and CO₂ carry near-zero GWP and no patent rent; R290 rose 11% quarter on quarter. OEM standardisation on naturals would compress the HFO premium

Fluorine's own regulatory overhang. The 2026 WMO/UNEP assessment terms of reference include early identification of substances of concern, naming TFA, a breakdown product associated with fluorinated gases. PFAS-adjacent action against HFOs would invert the trade, and Annex II gases would lose their scope advantage
Further US deregulation. EPA proposed on 26 May 2026 to exempt road and intermodal transport refrigeration units from AIM Act leak repair requirements, comments due 10 July 2026
Enforcement failure. Illegal import and quota fraud would leak the scarcity the case rests on; EPA has already applied administrative consequences to named entities

card.h1: Three scenario hypotheses, stated as hypotheses because no position data was supplied

ul.li: Base, the schedule holds. Assumption: the statutory 85% phasedown proceeds to 2036 while sector timing slips at the margin. Hypothesised effect: producer margin expansion continues at a decelerating rate and reclaim volumes scale. Test: quarterly regulated-segment margin versus group margin

Bull, GWP-linked pricing spreads. Assumption: other jurisdictions adopt quota pricing on the EU model. Hypothesised effect: the cost wedge widens and reclaim economics improve, since recycled material sits outside quota. Test: any second jurisdiction legislating a quota charge

Bear, naturals plus fluorine action. Assumption: OEM standardisation on propane and CO₂ coincides with regulatory action on fluorinated chemistry. Hypothesised effect: replacement-molecule pricing power compresses toward commodity economics while the cap still constrains legacy supply

card.p: Open question we are not answering today. Whether the bear case is a multiple de-rating or a franchise impairment depends on holdings, entry valuation and duration that were not provided. Treat both as live until the exposure screen is complete.

card.h1: Three decisions today, all of them about getting the facts before positioning

ol.li: Commission an exposure screen. Identify every holding with revenue or cost exposure to regulated refrigerants, split into producers, cooling-intensive operators, equipment OEMs and reclaim or servicing. Deliverable: names, weights, and the transmission channel for each. Owner: [name]. Date: [date]

Quantify pass-through. For cold chain, food retail and data-centre holdings, estimate refrigerant servicing cost per unit of capacity, separating EU quota-linked cost from market refrigerant price. Ask management three questions: current charge inventory by gas, replacement schedule, and contractual ability to pass cost through. Owner: [name]. Date: [date]

Scope reclaim before sizing it. Establish whether reclaimed volumes are genuinely outside quota in each jurisdiction we would invest in, and what the certification and collection economics are, before any capital is discussed. Owner: [name]. Date: [date]

card.p: Trip-wires for reconsideration: formal EU or EPA action naming TFA or HFOs under a PFAS framework; a natural-refrigerant standardisation announcement from two of the top five HVAC OEMs; or a sustained move in EU quota permit prices outside the €14 to €18.50 range.

brief.instruction: Institutional, evidential, plain-spoken. An investment committee memo, not a pitch. The audience is financially sophisticated and chemically illiterate: define GWP or R290 the first time in half a clause, never lecture. Target ~95 words per slide; the template holds median 98, p90 177, so budget 98 a slide and go to 177 only on a deliberately text-only slide such as the EU scope slide or the risk slide. Titles state the finding as a full sentence wherever the slide makes a point. Every slide carrying a figure ends in a source line naming the issuing body and date: EPA, the European Commission, EUR-Lex, the UNEP Ozone Secretariat, WMO, or the company filing. Numbers keep their units, their date and their comparison base: "up 22% year over year to $568M in Q1 2026", never "strong growth". Three registers must stay visibly distinct, and this is the point of the revision. Sourced fact reads flat and declarative with its citation. Derived arithmetic is introduced with an explicit marker such as "Illustrative" or "our calculation" and states the assumption it rests on. Interpretation is marked as ours ("our read", "our interpretation", "diligence question"). Never let a derived figure or a judgement inherit the tone of a sourced fact. No portfolio holdings, weights, valuations or positioning verdicts exist for this deck. Do not write that anything is under-owned, correctly sized, cheap, or that positioning is right. Where a portfolio number would belong, use a visibly bracketed placeholder such as [name] or [date], or convert the statement into a diligence question. Do not write investment advice or recommendations to buy, sell or reclassify. Vary sentence and paragraph length. No "Bold term: explanation" as a whole-slide pattern beyond the lead-in labels already in the outline. No signposting, no sweeping openers, no summary or inspirational closers, none of the "not just X, it's Y" contrast family, and no em dashes in body copy.

Three corrections from the previous draft are binding and must not be reintroduced by paraphrase. 1. The EU EUR 3 per tonne CO2 equivalent charge is a payment for allocated HFC quota under Article 17(5) of Regulation (EU) 2024/573, applying to hydrofluorocarbons listed in Annex I Section 1 and to quota for 2026 onward. It is not a levy on every F-gas placed on the market, it does not apply to PFCs, SF6 or NF3, and no indexation or permanence is stated anywhere in the Regulation or the Commission FAQ. Do not describe it as a permanent indexed levy, a tax on all F-gases, or a per-sale surcharge. 2. R1234yf is listed in Annex II as an unsaturated compound with GWP 0.501 and is outside the Annex I HFC quota system, so it carries no quota allocation payment. Do not state a EUR 0.002 per kg figure for it and do not state a 2,000-fold cost advantage over R134a. Its advantage is a scope exclusion. 3. HCFC phase-out differs by jurisdiction. Non-Article 5 parties reached 100% consumption reduction on 1 January 2020 with a 0.5% servicing allowance to 2030; Article 5 parties reach 100% on 1 January 2030 with a 2.5% servicing tail averaged over 2030 to 2040, running until 1 January 2040. Never write "complete global HCFC phase-out by 2030". The illustrative EUR/kg arithmetic on the EU scope slide and in its chart is our own derivation from the statutory rate, applies to Annex I HFCs only, and depends on Annex I content for blends. Label it as illustrative wherever it appears, including in the chart title and caption. Keep the EUR 3 statutory allocation payment visually and verbally separate from the EUR 14 to EUR 18.50 secondary quota permit market prices; they are different things and conflating them is a factual error.

Restrained consulting board pack. The template's navy ink, single blue accent, hairline rules and sourced footnotes carry the deck; density is the design. Give the most weight to three slides: the one-page summary as situation, complication, resolution bands with the reading-convention line held at the foot; the EU scope slide, where the in-scope and out-of-scope distinction is the argument and should be built as a two-column comparison or native table rather than a bullet run, with the illustrative chart clearly subordinate and captioned as derived; and the producer results slide, with big accent figures for 22%, 56% and 19% against flat group revenue. The scenarios slide wants three parallel stat columns headed Base, Bull and Bear, each visibly labeled as a hypothesis with its assumption, effect and test. The decisions slide wants numbered rows with owner and date tags. Use the template's hairline and label-tag vocabulary to mark register: give sourced facts, illustrative arithmetic and our interpretation visually distinct treatments, so a reader skimming can tell them apart without reading the qualifier. Imagery is sparse and documentary, in the template's evidence-photo register: cool daylight, steel-blue and grey, industrial cooling and infrastructure. Chiller plants, supermarket refrigeration, cold-storage interiors, a data-centre cooling hall. No stock-photo boardrooms, no polar bears, no melting ice, no glowing globes, nothing that reads as an environmental campaign. At most three or four photographs, each captioned as context rather than proof. No ozone-hole hero image; the satellite false-colour map is a cliché that signals the wrong genre for this audience.
